Empirical Research Plan ―  “Employment Effects of the ADA on Disabled Workers”

=======================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
=======================================================================
Method:  Difference-in-Differences (DID) augmented with event‐study dynamics
(TWFE and Sun-Abraham interaction-weighted estimators).

Why DID?  
• Treatment varies across groups (disabled vs. non-disabled) and over time
(pre- vs. post-ADA implementation in 1992).  
• The CPS provides repeated cross-sections on the same outcome variables for
treated and comparison groups over a long pre-period (mid-1980s) and post-period
(late-1990s), allowing a credible parallel-trends assessment.  
• The ADA was a nationwide federal shock, so cross-state variation is limited.
Group-level DID (plus rich covariates and fixed effects) is therefore the most
natural first-order design.  
• Event-study coefficients (“leads” and “lags”) reveal pre-trends and the
dynamic path of effects, strengthening causal interpretation.

Extension:  Where firm-size information is available or can be proxied,
estimate a triple-difference (DDD):  
(disabled – non-disabled) × (large-firm – small-firm) × (post-ADA).  
This exploits the > 15-employee coverage threshold in Title I of the ADA.

=======================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
=======================================================================
Treatment variable  
TREAT_i = 1 if individual i reports a work-limiting disability (CPS variable
 “disabwrk”) in survey year t.

Control group  
All working-age (21–58) individuals with no reported disability in year t.

Treatment timing  
POST_t = 1 for survey years 1992 and after; 0 for 1988–1991. (1985–1987 can
serve as additional pre-period for robustness; 1990–1991 are “anticipation” yrs
that can be omitted or coded separately.)

Outcome variables  
• EMPLOY_it  = 1 if employed in reference week  
• WEEKS_it   = weeks worked last year  
• LOGWAGE_it = log hourly wage (conditional on employment)

Covariates / fixed effects  
Age buckets, gender, race, education, industry, state, year.

No running variable ⇒ no RDD elements.

=======================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
=======================================================================
A1.  Parallel Trends  
In the absence of the ADA, employment outcomes for disabled and
non-disabled workers would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: use 5+ yrs of pre-ADA CPS to test; institutional
evidence suggests no other contemporaneous nationwide disability
legislation.

A2.  Stable Composition (no differential entry/exit)  
Disability self-reporting and survey sampling are stable across time.  
Plausibility: CPS disability module unchanged until 1994 redesign—include
year-specific controls; test for jumps in disability share.

A3.  No Anticipation / Minimal Anticipation  
Labor-market agents did not fully adjust behavior before 1992.  
Plausibility: ADA passed in mid-1990; include “anticipation” leads in event
study to verify small effects 1990–1991.

A4.  SUTVA / No Spillovers  
ADA’s effects on non-disabled outcomes do not contaminate disabled status
classification.  
Plausibility: reasonable because employment decisions are mostly individual.

=======================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
=======================================================================
T1.  Differential Macro Shocks  
Early-1990s recession may affect disabled workers differently.  
Mitigation: year fixed effects + state×year unemployment-rate controls; event
study to isolate ADA-specific break.

T2.  Measurement Change in Disability Variable (1994 CPS redesign).  
Mitigation: include year-specific dummies; re-estimate on balanced sample
1988–1993 (pre-redesign) and 1994–1998 separately; interact POST_t with dummy
for “new survey” to net out break.

T3.  Endogenous Reporting (strategic claiming of disability post-ADA).  
Mitigation: use “work-limiting” definition (less sensitive to incentives); show
results for alternative definition (activity limitation); employ bounding
exercises (Oster δ) on compositional changes.

=======================================================================
5. R Code Outline
=======================================================================
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # TWFE and Sun-Abraham
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load CPS micro data (assume stacked csv)
cps <- fread("cps_disability_1985_1998.csv")

# 2. Variable construction
cps[, post  := as.integer(year >= 1992)]
cps[, disabled := as.integer(disabwrk == 1)]
cps[, treat := disabled * post]

# Outcomes
cps[, employ := as.integer(lfs == "employed")]
cps[, logwage := log(hourly_wage)]
cps[, weeks := weeks_worked]

# Controls
cps[, age_cat := cut(age, c(21,40,59), labels = c("21_39","40_58"))]

# 3. Main DID specification (TWFE)
did_emp <- feols(employ ~ disabled*post + 
                 gender + race + educ + age_cat |
                 state + year, data = cps,
                 cluster = ~state)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham 2020 style)
cps[, rel_year := year - 1992]  # 1992 = 0
event_emp <- feols(employ ~ sunab(rel_year, disabled) +
                   gender + race + educ + age_cat |
                   state + year, data = cps, cluster = ~state)

# 5. Robustness: placebo law date (pretend law in 1988)
cps[, pseudo_post := as.integer(year >= 1988)]
placebo <- feols(employ ~ disabled*pseudo_post + 
                 gender + race + educ + age_cat |
                 state + year, data = cps, cluster = ~state)

# 6. Display
modelsummary(list(Main = did_emp, Event = event_emp, Placebo = placebo))
```

=======================================================================
6. Expected Results
=======================================================================
Theory is ambiguous: increased accommodation costs may discourage hiring
(Burkhauser et al. 2001), but stronger legal protections could raise retention
and participation.

Prior: Small to moderate negative employment effect on
disabled workers immediately after ADA (−2 to −4 percentage points on
employment-probability base of ~50 %), attenuating over time as labor markets
adjust.  Wage effects likely close to zero or slightly negative (costs partially
shifted into wages).

Heterogeneity:  
• Older (40-58) disabled more adversely affected than younger.  
• Gender gaps may widen if accommodation costs interact with gendered
occupational sorting.

=======================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
=======================================================================
C1.  Pre-Treatment Parallel Trends ….. 0.8 (visually plausible, some worry)  
C2.  No Differential Composition …….. 0.6 (survey redesign risk)  
C3.  No Simultaneous Confounders …… 0.8 (macro controls help)  
C4.  Stable Treatment Timing ……….. 0.9 (federal law, uniform start)  
C5.  Correct Functional Form ……….. 0.9 (linear prob TWFE + robustness)

Average score ≈ 0.8 ⇒ reasonably credible, but attention to measurement and
macro shocks is essential.
